title: Polish & UI
summary: Bring Kadi to life with Godot 4 Tweens: animate card deals, penalty stack pulses, and win-screen confetti — all without blocking the rules engine.

lessons.title: Animating Cards with Tweens
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Tweens

A **Tween** interpolates a property from one value to another over time. Godot 4's `create_tween()` returns a Tween you chain calls on — no manual `_process` math required.

```gdscript
func animate_deal(card_node: Node2D, target: Vector2) -> void:
    var start_pos: Vector2 = card_node.position
    card_node.position = start_pos + Vector2(0, -200)
    card_node.modulate.a = 0.0
    var tween: Tween = create_tween()
    tween.set_parallel(true)
    tween.tween_property(card_node, "position", target, 0.4) \
        .set_trans(Tween.TRANS_SINE) \
        .set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)
    tween.tween_property(card_node, "modulate:a", 1.0, 0.2)
    tween.chain().tween_callback(card_node.enable_input)
```

`set_parallel(true)` runs the position and alpha tweens simultaneously — the card flies in AND fades in together. `set_trans` picks the curve (`SINE` is smooth, `BACK` overshoots for a playful bounce). `set_ease` picks direction (`EASE_OUT` decelerates into the target, which feels natural for arrivals).

`chain()` forces the next tween to wait for the previous ones; here we enable input only after the card has landed.

To block on a tween, `await tween.finished` — useful when the rules engine must wait for an animation before advancing the turn.

> [!WHY]
> Tweens run on Godot's render loop, independent of the rules engine. The card visually flies in while the rules engine has already moved on — animations never block gameplay logic. Choosing `EASE_OUT` over linear interpolation is a deliberate feel choice: cards decelerate as they arrive, which reads as "settling" into the hand, far more satisfying than a robotic constant speed. The whole polish budget for Kadi is in these tiny curve choices; the rules are unaffected.

Keep tween durations under 0.5s — anything longer feels laggy in a turn-based game.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `pulse_penalty(label: Label)` that scales the label to 1.4 then back to 1.0, each over 0.15 seconds, using a Tween.
practicePrompt.hint: Use tween_property with "scale" and chain the two tweens.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does `set_parallel(true)` do on a Tween?
choices: Runs tweens on a separate thread
Runs subsequent tween calls simultaneously instead of sequentially
quizQuestions.explanation: `set_parallel(true)` makes chained tween_property calls overlap in time rather than queue one after another.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why choose `EASE_OUT` over linear interpolation for a card flying into the hand?
choices: It decelerates into the target, reading as the card "settling" — more natural and satisfying than constant speed
quizQuestions.explanation: Ease curves shape perceived motion. EASE_OUT slows the card as it arrives, mimicking physical deceleration and feeling far more polished.

lessons.title: Sound and Feedback

codeSnippets.caption: The feedback layer subscribes to rules-engine signals: sounds, a penalty flash, and a label.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write `_on_niko_announced(player: int)` that plays `niko_sound`, sets event_label to "NIKO KADI!", and pulses the label's scale to 1.5 and back with a Tween (0.15s each way).
practicePrompt.hint: Combine an AudioStreamPlayer.play() call with the pulse pattern from the Tweens lesson.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why connect the feedback layer to the rules engine's existing signals instead of calling `slap_sound.play()` inside `play_card()`?
choices: The rules engine stays feedback-agnostic: delete every sound node and the game still runs, and polish can be iterated with zero risk to the rules
play() cannot be called from the rules engine
quizQuestions.explanation: A one-way dependency keeps gameplay logic pure. The feedback layer is a listener you can rewrite freely — signals turn polish into a plug-in.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why pair every sound cue with a visual cue like the penalty flash?
choices: Players glance away and phones sit muted — redundant channels make sure the event lands even when one channel is missed
quizQuestions.explanation: Accessibility and real-world play conditions demand redundancy: the red flash communicates the penalty even at zero volume.

lessons.title: Exporting & Sharing Your Game
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Exporting & Sharing Your Game

Eleven phases ago, Kadi was a `var rank: int = 7`. Now it deals, jumps, kicks back, demands suits, announces "Niko Kadi", recycles its deck, and slaps cards with sound. One step remains: getting it off your machine and onto your friends' — because a card game with no opponents is just solitaire with extra rules.

First, download the **export templates**: `Editor > Manage Export Templates > Download and Install`. Templates are the precompiled Godot runtimes for each platform, matched to your editor version (4.3) — without them, no export.

Then open `Project > Export...` and click `Add...` to create a **preset** per platform. For Kadi three matter most: **Windows Desktop** produces an `.exe` you can zip and send; **Android** builds an `.apk` for the phones your friends actually carry (this one needs the Android SDK and a debug keystore — Godot's export dialog flags anything missing); **Web** exports an HTML5 build that runs in a browser, the lowest-friction way to share — upload to a host like itch.io and send a link.

Before exporting, make sure your game behaves like a finished product. A version label is the classic touch — and a reminder that `assert()` calls from Phase 10 vanish in release exports:

```gdscript
@onready var version_label: Label = $HUD/VersionLabel

func _ready() -> void:
    var version: String = ProjectSettings.get_setting("application/config/version", "1.0")
    version_label.text = "Kadi v%s (%s)" % [version, OS.get_name()]
    if OS.is_debug_build():
        version_label.text += " [debug]"
```

`OS.is_debug_build()` returns false in a release export — handy for hiding debug overlays and test buttons in the shipped game. Pick `Export Project...` in the preset dialog, choose a path, and Godot packs your scenes, scripts, and sounds into a single distributable build.

> [!WHY]
> Exporting early and often — not just at the end — catches platform-only bugs while they are cheap to fix: a touch input that works with a mouse but not a thumb, a font that renders differently on the web, a file path with the wrong case. More importantly, putting a build in a friend's hands closes the loop this whole course has been about: rules you encoded in Phase 0 booleans are now judged by a real player slapping a real (virtual) Joker down. That feedback is the most valuable test suite you will ever run.

Export the Windows build, zip it, and send it to someone who knows the game. When they argue about a rule, you can open the exact function that enforces it — you built every line.

codeSnippets.caption: A version label that also reveals whether you are running a debug or release build.

3. Fill preset options (Android needs SDK path + debug keystore)

5. Windows: zip the .exe + .pck | Android: install the .apk | Web: upload to itch.io

practicePrompt.instructions: Write `debug_tools_visible()` returning true only in debug builds, and use it in _ready() to hide a `test_panel` Control in release exports.
practicePrompt.hint: OS.is_debug_build() is the check; Control nodes have a `visible` property.

quizQuestions.prompt: What must be installed before Godot can export your project to ANY platform?
choices: The export templates matching your Godot version, via Editor > Manage Export Templates
quizQuestions.explanation: Export templates are the precompiled runtimes Godot wraps around your project. They are version-matched — 4.3 templates for a 4.3 editor — and required for every platform. The Android SDK is needed only for Android presets.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why export and share builds early rather than only when the game feels finished?
choices: Platform-only bugs (touch input, web fonts, path casing) surface while they are cheap to fix, and real players exercise the rules better than any test
quizQuestions.explanation: Each platform has quirks invisible in the editor. Frequent exports plus real players form a feedback loop no in-editor test can replace.
